chunks: "Isolation is important for safety, protection and noise.
Safety is the first one: if the power side has mains or even 48 volts and a person can touch the low-voltage side, like a USB port or a button, then a fault must not connect them.
That's the legal and standards-driven reason for isolating, with specified creepage and clearance and a rated barrier voltage. Second is protection.
In a motor drive, if a MOSFET fails short it can put the full motor supply on the gate, and through the gate resistor onto the MCU pin. A 3.
3 volt microcontroller won't survive 24 volts. An isolation barrier keeps the failure confined to the power side. Third is noise and ground.

If the motor current returns through the same ground trace as the microcontroller, then every PWM edge puts voltage on that shared return: 10 amps stepping in 100 nanoseconds through 10 nanohenries is a volt.
That shifts the MCU's ground relative to its signals and corrupts ADC readings and logic levels. Isolation lets the two grounds float relative to each other.
It also handles floating references, like a high-side driver or a current sensor on a switching node.
The trade-offs are cost, board area, and the need for an isolated power supply on one side.
There's propagation delay and limited bandwidth, which matters for fast control loops, and wear-out for optocouplers because the LED ages.
The barrier has capacitance, so fast common-mode transients still couple across, which is why the common-mode transient immunity spec matters.
And you need to respect creepage and clearance on the PCB.
So I'd isolate when there's a safety requirement, a hazardous voltage, or a really noisy or floating power stage, and not when a well-laid-out ground and a single low-voltage supply will do."
